qs.q: What is the primary role of hemoglobin in acid-base balance?
o: Eliminates carbon dioxide from the pulmonary alveoli
Regulates aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa
Acts as intracellular protein buffer binding hydrogen ions
Produces bicarbonate ions within the kidney tubules
qs.e: ** Hemoglobin acts as an intracellular protein buffer by binding with hydrogen ions, helping prevent large fluctuations in pH within red blood cells and contributing to overall buffering capacity.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Acid‑base balance keeps blood pH near 7.40 by coordinating respiratory CO₂ elimination and renal H⁺/HCO₃⁻ handling. Disruption leads to metabolic or respiratory acidosis/alkalosis, affecting cellular function.

sections.p: The body maintains a narrow pH range (7.35‑7.45) because enzyme activity and ion transport are pH‑sensitive. Two main systems—respiratory (CO₂) and renal (H⁺/HCO₃⁻)—work together to buffer acids and bases.

CO₂ combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (the Henderson‑Hasselbalch equation). Lungs control PaCO₂ by ventilation; kidneys control [HCO₃⁻] by reabsorption, generation, and acid excretion.
b: Renal H⁺ secretion ↔ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption (metabolic component)
Glutamine metabolism produces NH₃ and new HCO₃⁻

sections.p: Chemoreceptors sense pH/PaCO₂ and adjust ventilation within seconds. The kidneys respond over hours to days, using tubular transporters (NHE3, H⁺‑ATPase, NBCe1) and buffering systems.
b: Central chemoreceptors (medulla) respond to CSF pH
Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies) respond to arterial pH/PaCO₂
Kidney: three mechanisms – H⁺ secretion, HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, new HCO₃⁻ generation

sections.p: Acid‑base disorders arise when either the respiratory or renal component fails to compensate. They are classified by pH, primary disturbance, and compensation status.
b: Metabolic acidosis: low HCO₃⁻, low pH, e.g., DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure
Metabolic alkalosis: high HCO₃⁻, high pH, e.g., vomiting, diuretic use
Respiratory acidosis: high PaCO₂, low pH, e.g., COPD, severe asthma
Respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO₂, high pH, e.g., hyperventilation, high altitude

sections.p: Recognising the pattern guides urgent treatment—correcting the underlying cause, supporting ventilation or renal function, and avoiding harmful over‑correction.
b: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis can cause hypotension, arrhythmia, coma
Severe respiratory alkalosis may reduce cerebral blood flow, causing seizures
Pregnancy shifts normal values (PaCO₂ ↓, HCO₃⁻ ↓) – adjust interpretation

t.b: What is the primary disturbance and is compensation adequate? → Determines disorder type and severity
What is the anion gap? → Differentiates high‑anion‑gap vs. normal‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis
Is lactic acidosis contributing? → Guides source control and perfusion support

sections.p: Focus on interpreting ABG values, calculating the anion gap, and linking clinical scenarios to the appropriate disorder.
b: Anion gap = Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal 8‑12 mmol/L
Compensation formulas: e.g., expected PaCO₂ in metabolic acidosis = 1.5·[HCO₃⁻] + 8

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained respiratory failure with PaCO₂ >60 mmHg
Rapidly falling pH in a patient with DKA or sepsis

faq.q: Why does vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?
faq.a: Loss of gastric HCl reduces H⁺, raising HCO₃⁻ concentration and pH.

faq.q: Can a normal pH hide an acid‑base disorder?
faq.a: Yes, if a primary disturbance is fully compensated; ABG and anion gap reveal it.

faq.q: How does pregnancy affect ABG interpretation?
faq.a: PaCO₂ falls to ~30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ to ~20 mmol/L; pH remains normal.
